sentences.text: The skull of Sciurumimus is proportionally very large, measuring 156% of the femur length and extending further than the entire series of neck vertebrae.
This juvenile individual was approximately 72 centimeters long, possessing a tail composed of a total of 59 vertebrae.
Filamentous plumage preserved at the base of the tail and on other body parts gave the animal a shaggy appearance with a surface similar to skin.
The fossil is approximately 151 million years old and is considered one of the best-preserved dinosaur fossils in the world.
Its dentition is unique, as the first four upper jaw teeth lack serrations while the remaining 33 to 35 upper teeth are clearly serrated on the back edge and point strongly backward.
The only known specimen, catalogued as BMMS BK 11, was discovered between 2009 and 2010 during excavations at the Rygol limestone quarries near Painten in southern Germany.
Sciurumimus was first announced informally in 2011 but was not formally described and named until 2012 by Rauhut and colleagues.
Fossils dealer Raimund Albersdörfer funded the excavations, and his wife Birgit donated the fossil to the Solnhofen Mayor-Müller Museum as a permanent loan.
Young animals likely ate different food than adults.
Adult Sciurumimus likely reached a body length of 5 meters and possibly exhibited insular dwarfism.
Sciurumimus is classified within the superfamily Megalosauroidea, a group listed by the Paleobiology Database as its parent group.
An initial phylogenetic analysis suggested Sciurumimus was a primitive member of Megalosauroidea, a clade of large, primitive carnivorous dinosaurs.
In 2024, Andrea Cau recovered Sciurumimus, along with Compsognathus and Scipionyx, within different positions inside Megalosauroidea.
Sciurumimus lived at the end of the Jurassic period, approximately 150 million years ago during the Tithonian stage, in what is now Europe.
The fossil belongs to the beckeri zone of the Kimmeridgian stage, a period of the Late Jurassic.
Sciurumimus was originally classified as a basal megalosauroid, but later phylogenetic analyses disputed this placement.
Some analyses found Sciurumimus to be a compsognathid, though this position was noted as tentative.

Two other initial analyses, which the authors considered less well-founded, placed Sciurumimus closer to Monolophosaurus and Avetheropoda, or in an unresolved position between avetheropods and megalosauroids.
Many researchers criticized the initial study, noting that the data matrices used to connect the new fossil were incomplete and lacked relevant data from several species.
Other analyses suggested Sciurumimus was an allosauroid or a tetanuran outside of Avetheropoda.
Paul placed Sciurumimus as basal among the Maniraptoromorpha in 2016.
A detailed analysis of supplementary material found Sciurumimus to be a compsognathid, though the authors noted this position was tentative.
